summary: The Lord speaks to Moses from the Tabernacle, giving instructions for burnt offerings (v. 1). These offerings can be from cattle, flocks, or fowls (v. 2). The chapter details the specific procedures for preparing and sacrificing each type of animal, including who performs which step (vv. 3-17). The purpose of the offering is for atonement and to be a "sweet savour unto the Lord" (vv. 4, 9, 13, 17).
setting: The Lord speaks to Moses from the "tabernacle of the congregation" (v. 1). This setting suggests a time after the construction of the Tabernacle and before the Israelites settled in a permanent land. Most historians place this period during the Israelites' journey through the wilderness after their departure from Egypt.

events.what: The Lord calls to Moses from the Tabernacle.
The Lord instructs Moses to tell the Israelites about bringing offerings from cattle, flocks, or fowls.
If offering from the herd, the offerer brings a male animal without blemish to the Tabernacle door.
The offerer places their hand on the animal's head for atonement.
The offerer kills the animal, and priests sprinkle its blood on the altar.
The offerer skins and cuts the animal into pieces.
Priests prepare the altar fire and arrange the animal's parts (head, fat) on the wood.
The offerer washes the animal's inwards and legs, and the priest burns all on the altar as a "sweet savour".

If offering from the flock, the offerer brings a male animal without blemish, kills it north of the altar, and the priests sprinkle its blood; the offerer cuts it, and the priest burns it all on the altar as a "sweet savour".

If offering from fowls, the offerer brings turtledoves or young pigeons; the priest wrings off the bird's head, drains its blood, removes its crop and feathers, and burns the bird on the altar as a "sweet savour".

terms.meaning: A portable tent-like structure where the Lord's presence was said to dwell and where worship rituals were performed (v. 1).
An offering where the entire animal (or bird) is consumed by fire on the altar, except for specific parts like the crop and feathers of a bird (v. 3, 9, 15, 17).
An animal that is perfect, without any physical defect or imperfection (v. 3, 10).
A process by which an individual is made right with the Lord, often through a ritual act, resulting in acceptance (v. 4).
To remove the skin from an animal (v. 6).
A phrase describing the pleasing aroma of the burnt offering as it ascends to the Lord (v. 9, 13, 17).
A pouch in a bird's gullet where food is stored before digestion (v. 16).

readings.view: This chapter is understood as detailing the *olah* (burnt offering), one of several types of sacrifices commanded in the Torah. It emphasizes the complete devotion and surrender to God, as the entire animal is consumed on the altar.

Many Christians view these sacrificial laws as foreshadowing the sacrifice of Jesus Christ, who they believe fulfilled the need for such offerings. The "atonement" mentioned in v. 4 is often connected to Christ's atoning work.

Scholars often analyze Leviticus 1 within the context of ancient Near Eastern sacrificial practices, noting similarities and differences with rituals from surrounding cultures. They examine the text for insights into the development of Israelite religious practices and the priestly concerns of the time.

Samaritans, who accept the Torah as their holy scripture, follow the instructions for burnt offerings as literal divine commands, though the practice of animal sacrifice ceased with the destruction of their temple.

oftenQuoted.caution: The phrase "sweet savour unto the Lord" is sometimes quoted to describe something pleasing to God. However, in the surrounding text, it specifically refers to the pleasing aroma of a burnt animal offering consumed by fire on the altar, as part of a detailed ritual for atonement.
